title: The holy bond
hook: all things are woven together, and the bond is holy (Meditations 7.9)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the idle show, puppies and puppets and parades. Your line was good-natured. Did you stay kind in a silly scene? Day five hundred eighty-six.

Back in year one we met sympatheia, the Stoic idea that everything touches everything, and we traced a coffee cup back through a hundred pairs of hands. Today Marcus says the same thing again, in book seven, but he adds one word that changes the temperature. Connected is a fact, like plumbing. Marcus doesn't stop at connected. He calls the connection holy. That's a different kind of claim, and it asks something different of you.
screen: `SYMPATHEIA, REMEMBERED.` → `CONNECTED IS A FACT.` → `HE CALLS IT HOLY.`

segments.voice: First, the line. Meditations seven, nine, in George Long's translation: "All things are implicated with one another, and the bond is holy." Implicated is an old word for folded in together, like threads in cloth. Then he adds that hardly anything is foreign to anything else. Second, the list. Marcus keeps going, and the passage builds like a creed. One universe made of everything. One God running through everything. One substance, one law, one reason shared by every thinking creature, one truth. Whatever you believe about God, notice what he's doing. He's not describing a machine. He's describing something he reveres. Third, what holy adds. When something is holy, you don't just know about it. You handle it with care. You don't break it for convenience. So if the bond between you and others is holy, then cutting someone off out of spite, cheating a stranger you'll never see again, or talking about someone as if they were nothing isn't just unkind. For Marcus it's a kind of sacrilege, a tearing of something sacred. Fourth, where traditions meet. Many paths have their own words for a sacred web of relationship, each with its own meaning: covenant, communion, the body with many members, dependent arising. Those aren't the same teaching, and each tradition explains its own. Marcus's version is Stoic: a living cosmos with reason running through it. What they share is the instinct that our ties to each other aren't just useful. They're worth bowing to.
screen: `ALL THINGS FOLDED TOGETHER.` · `ONE UNIVERSE, ONE LAW, ONE REASON.` · `HOLY MEANS HANDLE WITH CARE.` · `OTHER PATHS, THEIR OWN WORDS.` · then, large: `THE HOLY BOND.`

segments.voice: Sit, and breathe. Think of one person you're tied to in a way you rarely notice. The neighbor whose name you know. A cousin far away. The person who drives your bus. Trace one thread between you: what they've given you, what you've given them, what you share. Then hold that thread the way you'd hold something sacred. Gently. Carefully. Just for the length of the sit. The bell holds the time.
The holy bond. Marcus's claim that everything is woven together, and that the weaving itself is sacred. Today's word.
Your line: the holy bond. Today, notice one moment when you're tempted to treat someone as if they didn't matter, and treat the tie between you with care instead. Day five hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus sometimes use 7.9 as a reminder that their ties to other people are not only practical but worth treating with reverence, especially toward strangers they'll never see again.
